node_definition: tip: Arawá, Juruá basin
event: Only record: 52-item wordlist collected by William Chandless on the Juruá in 1867, published 1869
controversy_notes: Date secure; data are tiny (52 items; only part of Dixon's 115-item list comparable), so tip is usable only with heavy missing data. Position: Dienst 2008 places it with Madi-Madihá on weak evidence.
original_source: Chandless, W. 1869. Notes of a journey up the River Juruá. J. Royal Geographical Society 39:296-311
dating_study: Dienst 2008 (classification only, no dating)

node_definition: tip: early Purus vocabularies
event: Paul Ehrenreich's Purus fieldwork (1889), published as 'Materialien zur Sprachenkunde Brasiliens: Vokabulare von Purus-Stämmen' (1897)
suggested_distribution: fixed_tip(61) only if the historical lect is coded separately; otherwise do not use
controversy_notes: Publication and 1889 Purus trip verified; which Arawan lects are included (Paumarí, Jamamadí assumed) NOT verified here. Modern Arawan data (Chapman & Derbyshire 1991, Dixon 2004, Dienst 2014) are effectively contemporary tips (age ~0 to -60).
original_source: Ehrenreich, P. 1897. Materialien zur Sprachenkunde Brasiliens: Vokabulare von Purus-Stämmen. Berlin: A. Asher

node_definition: MRCA(Arawá, Madi [Jarawara, Banawá, E. Jamamadí], Madihá [Kulina, Deni, W. Jamamadí], Paumarí, Suruwahá)
event: ASJP lexical-similarity date for Arauan: mean similarity 28.88 over 17 pairs, 4 of 5 Ethnologue subgroups; 1764 years before 2000
controversy_notes: Published estimate, benchmark only. ASJP dates miss calibrations by 29% on average (Holman et al. 2011); sd=500 reflects that. ASJP systematically underestimates old groups and tends to overestimate young ones. Circular if used as a calibration in a lexical-dating benchmark.
original_source: Holman et al. 2011 Current Anthropology 52(6):841-875 (ASJP)
dating_study: Holman et al. 2011 Current Anthropology 52(6):841-875 (ASJP)

node_definition: MRCA(all Arawan) — derived from Dixon's cognate percentages
event: Dixon (2004a:3) cognate percentages on a 115-item list: Madi-Arawá 79, Madihá-Arawá 72, Madi-Madihá 61, Paumarí-Arawá 54, Paumarí-Madi 50, Paumarí-Madihá 43, Suruwahá-Arawá 53, Suruwahá-Madi 37, Suruwahá-Madihá 34, Suruwahá-Paumarí 34. Naive Swadesh-Lees arithmetic on the deepest pairs (34%) gives c.2500 y (r=0.805/ky) to c.3600 y (r=0.86/ky)
suggested_distribution: not recommended as calibration; use only as a sanity range
evidence_type: inference (lexicostatistics; arithmetic done in this compilation)
controversy_notes: The percentages are published; the YEAR conversion is NOT published — it is computed here and inherits all glottochronology objections (non-Swadesh 115-item list, Arawá figures based on a partial list). Disagrees with ARW-003 (ASJP ~1700 y) by ~1-2 ky; together they bracket a plausible 1.5-3.5 ky depth.
original_source: Dixon, R.M.W. 2004. Proto-Arawá phonology. Anthropological Linguistics 46(1):1-83
dating_study: Dienst 2008 (reproduces the table)

target: Arawan root (upper bound on proto-Arawan emergence)
node_definition: MRCA(all Arawan)
event: Jolkesky's archaeo-ecolinguistic scenario: 'proto-proto-Arawa' and proto-Harakmbut-Katukina occupied contiguous areas on the right bank of the Solimões until the middle of the second half of the 2nd millennium BCE; proto-Arawa emerged later within the Central Amazon interaction sphere
controversy_notes: Qualitative scenario, not a date for proto-Arawan; Jolkesky himself rejects absolute dating of proto-languages. 3200 BP is this compilation's reading of 'meados da segunda metade do segundo milênio a.C.' (~1250 BCE). Depends on the contested Arawa-Harakmbut-Katukina contact/relationship hypothesis.
original_source: Jolkesky, M.P.V. 2016. Estudo arqueo-ecolinguístico das terras tropicais sul-americanas. PhD thesis, Universidade de Brasília, §5.3.6 (repositorio.unb.br/handle/10482/21671)

event: Root prior used by Greenhill et al. 2017; mean equals Gray et al. 2009 posterior (5230 BP, 95% HPD 4750-5800)
controversy_notes: Circular if reused on ABVD data: the prior is itself a posterior of Gray 2009. Use only as a benchmark, not as a calibration, for Austronesian; acceptable as a cross-family rate-prior anchor with caution. min/max = mean +/- 2 sd.

node_definition: MRCA of all Austronesian, assuming Taiwan homeland
event: Onset of Taiwanese Neolithic (Dabenkeng/Tapenkeng culture) c. 5500-5000 BP, interpreted as arrival of pre-/early Austronesian speakers
controversy_notes: Only a maximum if PAn diversified in Taiwan after Neolithic arrival (Out-of-Taiwan model). Wikipedia/secondary ranges vary (c. 4000-3000 BC vs 5500-5000 BP); exact calibrated range from Hung & Carson 2014 not verified here.
original_source: Hung H-c, Carson MT 2014 Antiquity 88:1115-1131 'Foragers, fishers and farmers: origins of the Taiwanese Neolithic'

node_definition: MRCA of all Malayo-Polynesian languages (e.g. Tagalog, Malagasy, Chamorro, Fijian)
event: Austronesian entry into the Philippines (Gray 2009: 3600-4500 BP, after Pawley 2002); Greenhill 2017 recast as Normal(4000,250)
controversy_notes: Gray 2010 (PLoS ONE) excluded it from the 'robust' set as contestable (red-slipped pottery = Austronesian arrival). Cochrane et al. 2021 model initial pottery in N Luzon at 5430-4290 cal BP (Nagsabaran 5440-4270), older than this range; Batan Island charcoal-only 3380-2590 cal BP. Gray 2009 reports root age barely changed (5230 vs 5230) without this constraint. Gray 2009 Table S3 ages are 'years before present' as published (not explicitly 1950-based; Favorlang/Siraya 346-384 implies a c. 2000-2010 basis, so subtract c. 50-60 y for 1950 basis). Values reproduced via Kaiping et al. burstclock supplement (github Anaphory/burstclock add_calibrations.py) because Science SOM was not retrievable; treat exact numbers as verified-secondary.
original_source: Pawley A 2002, in Bellwood & Renfrew (eds) Examining the farming/language dispersal hypothesis, McDonald Institute
dating_study: Gray RD, Drummond AJ, Greenhill SJ 2009 Science 323:479-483 (SOM Table S3); Greenhill SJ et al. 2017 PNAS (Evolutionary dynamics of language systems; normal priors)

node_definition: Settlement of Batanes by MP (Batanic) speakers; bound on lineage leading to Ivatan/Itbayaten
event: Initial pottery in Batanes: Itbayat 5200-3990 cal BP; Batan 3380-2590 cal BP (charcoal only) or 3640-2890 (incl. residues); Sunget 4330-2890 (95% HPD)
controversy_notes: Authors flag Batanes and Luzon ranges as less reliable than Mussau/Flores suites; pottery-language association assumed..
original_source: Cochrane EE, Rieth TM, Filimoehala D 2021 PLoS ONE 16(6):e0251407

node_definition: MRCA of all Oceanic languages
event: Development of Proto-Oceanic linked to Lapita in the Bismarck Archipelago (Gray 2009: 3200-3600 BP, after Lynch, Ross & Crowley 2002); Greenhill 2017 Normal(3300,100)
controversy_notes: One of Gray et al. 2010's five 'least controversial' calibrations. Conflict: Gray, Atkinson & Greenhill 2011 (Phil Trans B) phrase it as arrival in Oceania 3000-3300 BP. Archaeological Lapita onset (Denham et al. 2012) 3470-3250 cal BP Mussau. PO may predate Lapita pottery (pre-Lapita Austronesian presence) or post-date it. Gray 2009 Table S3 ages are 'years before present' as published (not explicitly 1950-based; Favorlang/Siraya 346-384 implies a c. 2000-2010 basis, so subtract c. 50-60 y for 1950 basis). Values reproduced via Kaiping et al. burstclock supplement (github Anaphory/burstclock add_calibrations.py) because Science SOM was not retrievable; treat exact numbers as verified-secondary.
original_source: Lynch J, Ross M, Crowley T 2002 The Oceanic Languages (Curzon)
dating_study: Gray RD, Drummond AJ, Greenhill SJ 2009 Science 323:479-483 (SOM Table S3); Greenhill SJ, Drummond AJ, Gray RD 2010 PLoS ONE 5(3):e9573; Greenhill SJ et al. 2017 PNAS (Evolutionary dynamics of language systems; normal priors)

node_definition: MRCA of all Oceanic languages
event: Emergence of Lapita pottery: Mussau 3470-3250 cal BP; rest of Bismarck Archipelago 3360-3240 cal BP (OxCal Bayesian model)
controversy_notes: Rieth & Athens 2017/2019 (J Island Coastal Archaeol 14:5-16, doi 10.1080/15564894.2017.1331939) give Bismarck Lapita onset 3535-3234 cal BP (95%) per secondary citation, not verified. Cochrane et al. 2021: Mussau island-wide 3470-3010. Mapping PO = Lapita onset is an assumption.
original_source: Denham T, Bronk Ramsey C, Specht J 2012 Archaeology in Oceania 47(1):39-46

node_definition: MRCA of Fijian, Rotuman and Polynesian languages
event: Proto-Central Pacific, prior from Greenhill et al. 2017 (following Gray 2009) Normal(3000,100)
controversy_notes: Must be younger than Fiji settlement (AN-008); Normal(3000,100) puts some mass before Petchey 2015's Fiji range (3020-2860). Not in Gray 2009 Table S3 as listed in burstclock; appears in Greenhill 2017.
original_source: Gray RD, Drummond AJ, Greenhill SJ 2009 Science 323:479-483 (SOM Table S3)
dating_study: Greenhill SJ et al. 2017 PNAS (Evolutionary dynamics of language systems; normal priors)

node_definition: MRCA of Fijian + Polynesian (+Rotuman); bound from first settlement of Fiji
event: Lapita arrival in Fiji: 3130-3010 cal BP (Denham et al. 2012); 3020-2860 cal BP (as cited by Petchey et al. 2015)
controversy_notes: Two estimates disagree by c. 100-150 y. Bound is a maximum for Central Pacific diversification (cannot diversify before Fiji is reached).
original_source: Denham T, Bronk Ramsey C, Specht J 2012 Archaeology in Oceania 47:39-46; Petchey F et al. 2015 J Archaeol Sci Reports (Teouma chronology)

target: Vanuatu Oceanic languages (North-Central Vanuatu + Southern Vanuatu)
node_definition: Diversification of Oceanic languages of Vanuatu
event: First settlement of Efate (Teouma Lapita site): modelled start 2920-2870 cal BP (68%), deposits 3000-2560; cemetery in use from c. 2940-2880 cal BP; Denham et al. 2012 give Vanuatu 3250-3100 cal BP
controversy_notes: aDNA shows near-complete population turnover in Vanuatu after Lapita (Posth et al. 2018 Nat Ecol Evol) with Austronesian languages retained, so language-population continuity debated; Vanuatu languages may not form a single clade (no glottocode given).
original_source: Petchey F, Spriggs M, Bedford S, Valentin F 2015 J Archaeol Sci Reports (2015); Petchey F et al. 2014 J Archaeol Sci (Teouma burials)

controversy_notes: Polynesian diversification must post-date settlement of Tonga; Proto-Polynesian developed during a long 'Ancestral Polynesian' period in Tonga-Samoa so the node is likely much younger (bound is loose). Petchey 2015 cites Tonga colonisation 2850-2830 cal BP. Burley et al. 2015 PLoS ONE (doi 10.1371/journal.pone.0120795) refine Tongan settlement sequence.

Using Gray 2009 range inflates Polynesian ages. Retain only for replicating Gray 2009. Gray 2009 Table S3 ages are 'years before present' as published (not explicitly 1950-based; Favorlang/Siraya 346-384 implies a c. 2000-2010 basis, so subtract c. 50-60 y for 1950 basis). dating_study: Gray RD, Drummond AJ, Greenhill SJ 2009 Science 323:479-483 (SOM Table S3)

node_definition: MRCA of East Polynesian languages
event: Earliest settlement of East Polynesia: Society Islands AD c. 1025-1120 (short-lived samples), i.e. 925-830 BP
controversy_notes: Maximum for EP diversification under the short chronology. Some argue for earlier occupation (e.g. Hawaii AD 940-1130, Athens et al. 2014), which would push the bound to c. 1010 BP; Gambier 1108-1275 ambiguous.
original_source: Wilmshurst JM, Hunt TL, Lipo CP, Anderson AJ 2011 PNAS 108(5):1815-1820

node_definition: MRCA of Rapanui and Central-Eastern Polynesian
event: Settlement of Rapa Nui AD c. 1200-1253 (Wilmshurst 2011); c. AD 1200 (Hunt & Lipo 2006) -> Rapanui lineage separated no later than this
controversy_notes: Requires Rapanui to be the first offshoot of EP (standard subgrouping) and no later re-contact. Combined with AN-014 brackets PEP at c. 700-930 BP.
original_source: Hunt TL, Lipo CP 2006 Science 311:1603-1606; Wilmshurst JM, Hunt TL, Lipo CP, Anderson AJ 2011 PNAS 108(5):1815-1820

node_definition: Split of Hawaiian from closest EP relatives (Marquesan, Mangarevan)
event: Settlement of Hawaii: AD c. 1219-1266 (Wilmshurst 2011) vs AD 940-1130 (95% HPD; Athens, Rieth & Dye 2014)
controversy_notes: Two chronologies differ by 100-300 y. Hawaiian may have had later Tahitian contact (traditions; lexical borrowing), so split may be younger than settlement - weak minimum.
original_source: Wilmshurst JM, Hunt TL, Lipo CP, Anderson AJ 2011 PNAS 108(5):1815-1820; Athens JS, Rieth TM, Dye TS 2014 American Antiquity 79(1):144-155

node_definition: Split of New Zealand Maori from Cook Islands Maori/Tahitian
event: Settlement of New Zealand AD c. 1230-1282 (Wilmshurst 2011); rat-gnawed seeds/bones post-date c. AD 1280 (Wilmshurst et al. 2008)
controversy_notes: Robust settlement date; as a language split it assumes no post-settlement contact (voyaging to/from NZ probably continued briefly). Also a maximum for Maori dialect diversification.
original_source: Wilmshurst JM, Hunt TL, Lipo CP, Anderson AJ 2011 PNAS 108(5):1815-1820; Wilmshurst JM et al. 2008 PNAS 105(22):7676-7680

node_definition: Split of Moriori (Chatham Is.) from NZ Maori
event: Settlement of Rekohu (Chatham Islands): earliest reliable 14C on kopi seed cal AD 1450-1620 (95%); commonly cited c. AD 1500. Maximum is NZ settlement (c. AD 1280)
controversy_notes: Traditions, Moriori-Maori dialect differences and archaic artefacts have been argued to indicate 13th-c. settlement; radiocarbon supports 15th-16th c. Moriori assumed derived from NZ Maori; Moriori data are sparse 19th-c. records.
original_source: Barber IG, Maxwell JJ, Petchey F 2016 J Archaeol Sci Reports 10:96-109

node_definition: Settlement of the Marquesas (min for Marquesic lineage split from Tahitic)
event: Settlement of the Marquesas AD 1200-1277
controversy_notes: Earlier claims of Marquesan settlement c. 2000 BP (long chronology) are rejected by Wilmshurst 2011.
original_source: Wilmshurst JM, Hunt TL, Lipo CP, Anderson AJ 2011 PNAS 108(5):1815-1820

node_definition: MRCA of Nuclear Micronesian languages (Chuukic, Pohnpeic, Kosraean, Marshallese, Kiribati)
event: Settlement of (eastern) Micronesia 1900-2200 BP (Gray 2009, after Pawley 2002); Greenhill 2017 Normal(2000,100)
controversy_notes: Atoll settlement after mid-Holocene highstand; Micronesian diversification probably post-dates arrival. Gray 2009 Table S3 ages are 'years before present' as published (not explicitly 1950-based; Favorlang/Siraya 346-384 implies a c. 2000-2010 basis, so subtract c. 50-60 y for 1950 basis). Values reproduced via Kaiping et al. burstclock supplement (github Anaphory/burstclock add_calibrations.py) because Science SOM was not retrievable; treat exact numbers as verified-secondary.
original_source: Pawley A 2002 (see AN-003)
dating_study: Gray RD, Drummond AJ, Greenhill SJ 2009 Science 323:479-483 (SOM Table S3); Greenhill SJ et al. 2017 PNAS (Evolutionary dynamics of language systems; normal priors)

node_definition: Split of Chamorro from its closest Malayo-Polynesian relatives (Philippine/Western MP)
event: Initial settlement of the Mariana Islands c. 1500 BC (Carson; earliest Unai Bapot ranges 1916-1558 cal BC, preferred 1612-1558 BC)
controversy_notes: Rieth & Athens 2017/2019 Bayesian model argue for a later (Lapita-contemporaneous) Marianas settlement - exact range not verified here. Chamorro has a later Philippine/Latte-period overlay; linguistic link of first settlers uncertain (aDNA Pugach et al. 2021 PNAS links to Philippines). Min = split no later than settlement only if Chamorro descends from first settlers.
original_source: Carson MT 2020 Radiocarbon 62(6):1733-1754

node_definition: MRCA of Chamic languages (Cham, Jarai, Rade, Roglai, Tsat; excl. Acehnese)
event: Chamic speakers described in Chinese records c. 1800 BP and probable entry into Vietnam c. 2600 BP: Gray 2009 range 1800-2500 BP (after Thurgood 1999)
controversy_notes: Maurits et al. 2020 criticise this: Chinese records attest the polity (Linyi/Champa), not a unified Proto-Chamic language, so the bound is unjustified. Also note Gray 2010 listed Chamic among calibrations dropped from the robust set. Gray 2009 Table S3 ages are 'years before present' as published (not explicitly 1950-based; Favorlang/Siraya 346-384 implies a c. 2000-2010 basis, so subtract c. 50-60 y for 1950 basis). Values reproduced via Kaiping et al. burstclock supplement (github Anaphory/burstclock add_calibrations.py) because Science SOM was not retrievable; treat exact numbers as verified-secondary.
original_source: Thurgood G 1999 From Ancient Cham to Modern Dialects (Oceanic Linguistics Special Publication 28, Univ. Hawai'i Press)
dating_study: Gray RD, Drummond AJ, Greenhill SJ 2009 Science 323:479-483 (SOM Table S3); critique: Maurits L et al. 2020 J Lang Evol 5(1):17-38

node_definition: MRCA of Malayic and Chamic (incl. Acehnese)
event: Existence of Malayo-Chamic subgroup 2000-3000 BP (Gray 2009, after Thurgood 1999)
controversy_notes: Burstclock maps to 'North and East Malayo-Sumbawan' (nort3170, not in current Glottolog); current Glottolog node is Malayo-Chamic mala1554. Inferential, weakly justified. Gray 2009 Table S3 ages are 'years before present' as published (not explicitly 1950-based; Favorlang/Siraya 346-384 implies a c. 2000-2010 basis, so subtract c. 50-60 y for 1950 basis). Values reproduced via Kaiping et al. burstclock supplement (github Anaphory/burstclock add_calibrations.py) because Science SOM was not retrievable; treat exact numbers as verified-secondary.
original_source: Thurgood G 1999 (as AN-022)
dating_study: Gray RD, Drummond AJ, Greenhill SJ 2009 Science 323:479-483 (SOM Table S3)

node_definition: Old Cham, earliest attested Chamic language
event: Dong Yen Chau inscription (near Tra Kieu, Vietnam), undated but late 4th c. AD by match with dated Sanskrit inscriptions of Bhadravarman I; widely cited as the oldest text in any Austronesian language
controversy_notes: Dating is paleographic/contextual, not absolute; text is short. Also implies Chamic lineage (and possibly Proto-Chamic) older than c. 1600 BP. Thurgood regards the Tra Kieu-area inscription as the earliest Austronesian document. Glottocode for Old Cham not verified.
original_source: Coedès G 1939 (BEFEO 39); Thurgood G 1999

node_definition: Old Malay, Srivijaya inscriptions
event: Kedukan Bukit inscription (Palembang), Saka 604/605 = AD 682/683; earliest dated Old Malay text
controversy_notes: Year reading Saka 604 vs 605 (AD 682 vs 683) differs between sources; immaterial. Other Srivijaya inscriptions (Talang Tuwo 684, Kota Kapur 686) corroborate.
original_source: Coedès G 1930 BEFEO 30 (Les inscriptions malaises de Çrivijaya)

node_definition: Old Javanese (Kawi)
event: Old Javanese as spoken/written 700-1200 BP (Gray 2009 tip calibration, after Zoetmulder 1982); earliest wholly Javanese inscription Sukabumi, 25 March AD 804 (1146 BP)
controversy_notes: One of Gray 2010's five robust calibrations. Literary Old Javanese corpus spans 9th-15th c.; choose range matching the lexical source used (Zoetmulder dictionary = mostly 10th-14th c. literature). Gray 2009 Table S3 ages are 'years before present' as published (not explicitly 1950-based; Favorlang/Siraya 346-384 implies a c. 2000-2010 basis, so subtract c. 50-60 y for 1950 basis). Values reproduced via Kaiping et al. burstclock supplement (github Anaphory/burstclock add_calibrations.py) because Science SOM was not retrievable; treat exact numbers as verified-secondary.
original_source: Zoetmulder PJ 1982 Old Javanese-English Dictionary (KITLV)
dating_study: Gray RD, Drummond AJ, Greenhill SJ 2009 Science 323:479-483 (SOM Table S3); Greenhill, Drummond & Gray 2010 PLoS ONE

node_definition: MRCA of Javanese varieties (Javanesic)
event: Proto-Javanese 1100-1300 BP (Gray 2009 Table S3, after Zoetmulder 1982 and Anderson & Sinoto 2002 as cited)
controversy_notes: Justification thin: Old Javanese texts imply Javanese lineage existed by then; making it the MRCA of modern Javanese varieties assumes those varieties diverged after Old Javanese. Inconsistent with treating Old Javanese (700-1200) as a descendant tip. Gray 2009 Table S3 ages are 'years before present' as published (not explicitly 1950-based; Favorlang/Siraya 346-384 implies a c. 2000-2010 basis, so subtract c. 50-60 y for 1950 basis). Values reproduced via Kaiping et al. burstclock supplement (github Anaphory/burstclock add_calibrations.py) because Science SOM was not retrievable; treat exact numbers as verified-secondary.
original_source: Zoetmulder 1982
dating_study: Gray RD, Drummond AJ, Greenhill SJ 2009 Science 323:479-483 (SOM Table S3)

node_definition: MRCA of Malagasy dialects
event: Settlement of Madagascar 1100-1300 BP (Gray 2009, after Verin & Wright 1999); Asian crops (rice, mung bean, cotton) dominate Madagascar/Comoros sites from c. AD 700-900 (Crowther et al. 2016)
controversy_notes: Settlement is logically a maximum for Malagasy dialect diversification, not a node age. Serva et al. 2012 (lexicostatistics) date Indonesian colonisation c. AD 650. Earlier forager presence (Dewar et al. 2013) irrelevant to the Austronesian arrival. Gray 2009 Table S3 ages are 'years before present' as published (not explicitly 1950-based; Favorlang/Siraya 346-384 implies a c. 2000-2010 basis, so subtract c. 50-60 y for 1950 basis). Values reproduced via Kaiping et al. burstclock supplement (github Anaphory/burstclock add_calibrations.py) because Science SOM was not retrievable; treat exact numbers as verified-secondary.
original_source: Verin P, Wright H 1999 (as cited in Gray 2009 SOM; full reference not verified); Crowther A et al. 2016 PNAS 113(24):6635-6640
dating_study: Gray RD, Drummond AJ, Greenhill SJ 2009 Science 323:479-483 (SOM Table S3); Serva M, Petroni F, Volchenkov D, Wichmann S 2012 J R Soc Interface 9(66):54-67

node_definition: MRCA of Malagasy and Ma'anyan
event: Malagasy separated from Ma'anyan no later than the Austronesian settlement of Madagascar (crops AD 700-900; Serva 2012 c. AD 650)
controversy_notes: Assumes Malagasy migrants left Borneo after the Malagasy-Ma'anyan split began (Dahl 1951; Adelaar). Adelaar argues migration was led by Malay speakers from Sumatra (Malay/Javanese loans), so departure may post-date the split substantially.
original_source: Crowther A et al. 2016 PNAS 113(24):6635-6640
dating_study: Serva M et al. 2012 J R Soc Interface 9:54-67

node_definition: Favorlang (Babuza), extinct Formosan
event: Happart's Favorlang dictionary manuscript, 1650 (Gray 2009 used 346-384 BP 'age of source data')
controversy_notes: Gray et al. 2010 robust set. Burstclock excluded Favorlang because ABVD data mix mid-1600s Dutch sources with c. 1900 wordlists - check the source of each item before using.
original_source: Happart G 1650 (ms; publ. Medhurst 1840, Campbell 1896)
dating_study: Gray RD, Drummond AJ, Greenhill SJ 2009 Science 323:479-483 (SOM Table S3); Greenhill et al. 2010

node_definition: Siraya, extinct Formosan
event: Gravius' Siraya Gospels of Matthew and John (Amsterdam 1661) and Catechism (1662); Gray 2009 used 346-384 BP
controversy_notes: Gray et al. 2010 robust set. 1950-basis ages here computed from 1661-1662; Gray's 346-384 BP is on a present (c. 2000s) basis.
original_source: Gravius D 1661 Het Heylige Euangelium Matthei en Johannis (Amsterdam)
dating_study: Gray RD, Drummond AJ, Greenhill SJ 2009 Science 323:479-483 (SOM Table S3); Greenhill et al. 2010

node_definition: Early Malagasy (northeastern coastal dialect)
event: Frederick de Houtman, Spraeck ende Woord-boeck inde Maleysche ende Madagaskarsche Talen, Amsterdam 1603 (Dutch-Malagasy vocabulary)
controversy_notes: Small vocabulary; dialect not Plateau Malagasy (plat1254). Useful only if a 1603 Malagasy wordlist is included as a tip.
original_source: de Houtman F 1603 (Amsterdam); Glottolog reference 18058

node_definition: Early Tagalog
event: Doctrina Christiana en lengua espanola y tagala, Manila 1593 (first book printed in the Philippines)
controversy_notes: Date well established; lexical content limited (religious text). Not independently re-verified via web in this session.
original_source: Doctrina Christiana 1593 (Manila)

node_definition: Early Chamorro
event: San Vitores, Gramatica y Doctrina Christiana de la Lengua Mariana, 1668
controversy_notes: Date and title from memory; not verified in this session.
original_source: San Vitores DL 1668

node_definition: Arrival of pottery-using (presumed MP-speaking) groups in Sulawesi (Minanga Sipakko)
event: Initial pottery Sulawesi island-wide 4550-3590 cal BP; Minanga Sipakko 4600-3510 cal BP (95% HPD)
controversy_notes: Maximum for diversification of Sulawesi MP subgroups if pottery = Austronesian arrival; association contested (multi-directional Neolithic dispersal argued by the authors).
original_source: Cochrane EE, Rieth TM, Filimoehala D 2021 PLoS ONE 16(6):e0251407

node_definition: Sensitivity benchmark: Austronesian root age on 'robust' calibration subset (Proto-Oceanic, Old Javanese, Old Chinese outgroup, Favorlang, Siraya)
event: Benchmark result: root mean 5117 BP, 95% HPD 4660-5680 BP with five least controversial calibrations (vs 5230, 4750-5800 with full set)
controversy_notes: Held-out benchmark, not a calibration. Old Chinese (2300-2900 BP) was used as the Sino-Tibetan outgroup tip in Gray 2009.
original_source: Greenhill SJ, Drummond AJ, Gray RD 2010 PLoS ONE 5(3):e9573
dating_study: Gray RD, Drummond AJ, Greenhill SJ 2009 Science 323:479-483 (SOM Table S3)

node_definition: MRCA of Inuit varieties east of the Mackenzie delta (Inuinnaqtun, Eastern Canadian Inuktitut, Kalaallisut, Tunumiisut, Inuktun)
event: Thule (ancestral Inuit) expansion from Alaska into the Canadian Arctic; no secure Thule occupation in western Canadian Arctic before 13th c. CE (Friesen & Arnold 2008); Greenland reached c. 1300 CE
controversy_notes: Older 'c. 1000 CE' Thule chronology (pre-McGhee 2000) would push the bound to ~950 BP; Raghavan et al. 2014 aDNA consistent with recent Thule spread. Bound applies to the eastern dialect chain only, not to Alaskan Inupiaq.
original_source: Friesen & Arnold 2008, The timing of the Thule migration: new dates from the western Canadian Arctic, American Antiquity 73(3):527-538
dating_study: Raghavan et al. 2014, The genetic prehistory of the New World Arctic, Science 345:1255832

node_definition: MRCA of all Inuit languages (Alaskan Inupiaq through Greenlandic)
event: Proto-Inuit = Birnirk/Thule horizon of northern Alaska; ASJP calibration 'Inuit' = 800 years
controversy_notes: Holman et al. value (800) is in years before c. 2000 CE, i.e. ~750 BP(1950). Fortescue et al. (CED) put Proto-Inuit at ~1000 years (secondary report, unverified). ASJP estimated 945, GBD 1710 (Rama & Wichmann 2020 Table 5) - a held-out benchmark that GBD badly overshoots.
original_source: Holman et al. 2011, Automated dating of the world's language families based on lexical similarity, Current Anthropology 52(6):841-875 (calibration value as tabulated in Rama & Wichmann 2020 Table 1)
dating_study: Rama & Wichmann 2020, A test of Generalized Bayesian dating, PLOS ONE 15(8):e0236522

node_definition: MRCA of Yupik languages (Central Alaskan Yup'ik, Siberian Yupik, Alutiiq) and Inuit; Sirenik placement unresolved
event: Proto-Eskimo split into Yupik and Inuit branches
controversy_notes: Alaska Native Language Center states ~1000 years ago; secondary reports attribute ~2000 years to Proto-Eskimo (Fortescue, Jacobson & Kaplan, Comparative Eskimo Dictionary 1994/2010) - exact wording not verified. Old Bering Sea/Norton correlations are often invoked. Treat as weak.
original_source: Fortescue, Jacobson & Kaplan 1994 (2nd ed. 2010), Comparative Eskimo Dictionary with Aleut Cognates, ANLC Fairbanks

node_definition: MRCA of Aleut (aleu1260) and Eskimo (Yupik+Inuit)
event: Proto-Eskimo-Aleut divergence into Aleut and Eskimo
controversy_notes: Bergsland 1986 gives 4000-2000 BCE (via Wikipedia, not checked in original); ANLC: 'at least 4,000 years ago'; Berge 2018 (per ICHL26 handout) 6000-4000 BP for Proto-Eskaleut. Palaeo-Eskimo/Neo-Eskimo genetic links (Flegontov et al. 2019 Nature, 10.1038/s41586-019-1251-y) are argued to fit an Eskaleut spread but do not fix the date.
original_source: Bergsland 1986, Comparative Eskimo-Aleut phonology and lexicon, Journal de la Societe Finno-Ougrienne 80:63-137
dating_study: Flegontov et al. 2019 (genetic correlate, not a linguistic date)

node_definition: tip: 18th-c. West Greenlandic
event: Poul Egede, Dictionarium Groenlandico-Danico-Latinum (Copenhagen 1750); Grammatica Groenlandica Danico-Latina 1760
controversy_notes: Only useful if 18th-c. lexical forms are coded as a separate tip from modern Kalaallisut; orthography pre-Kleinschmidt.
original_source: Egede, P. 1750. Dictionarium Groenlandico-Danico-Latinum. Copenhagen

node_definition: MRCA of Apachean (Navajo nava1243, Western Apache, Chiricahua, Mescalero, Jicarilla, Lipan, Plains Apache) and Northern Athabaskan
event: Coronado expedition meets bison-hunting 'Querechos' on the Southern Plains (1541), generally identified as Apacheans; possible Apachean ancestors at Promontory Caves, Utah, c. 13th c. CE (Ives et al.)
controversy_notes: Querechos=Apache identification is standard but not certain; Promontory attribution (Ives, Janetski) is argued, not proven. Hoijer 1956 glottochronology gives relative Athabaskan chronology (numbers not checked here). The split is certainly older than the attestation; upper end of range is a guess bounded by Proto-Athabaskan, not a published figure.
original_source: Hammond & Rey (eds.) Coronado expedition narratives (1540-42); Ives et al. Promontory Caves project (Univ. Alberta)
dating_study: Hoijer 1956, The chronology of the Athapaskan languages, IJAL 22(4):219-232

node_definition: MRCA of Apachean languages (Navajo, Western Apache, Chiricahua, Mescalero, Jicarilla, Lipan, Plains Apache)
event: Apachean arrival in the Southwest/Southern Plains, usually placed c. 1300-1500 CE; no secure archaeological evidence before c. 1400 in many areas
controversy_notes: Arrival dates are disputed (writers 'disagree widely' per NPS Canyon de Chelly history); some Apachean diversification may predate arrival (Plains Apache/Kiowa-Apache is the deepest split), so the bound is weak. Sources cited here are secondary (NPS); primary: Seymour (ed.) 2012 'From the Land of Ever Winter to the American Southwest' (Univ. of Utah Press) - not checked.
original_source: Seymour (ed.) 2012, From the Land of Ever Winter to the American Southwest: Athapaskan Migrations, Mobility, and Ethnogenesis

node_definition: MRCA of Northern Wakashan (Kwak'wala, Heiltsuk, Haisla, Oowekyala) and Southern Wakashan (Nuu-chah-nulth, Ditidaht, Makah)
event: ASJP calibration 'Wakashan' = 2500 years
evidence_type: archaeology/inference (basis in Holman et al. not checked)
controversy_notes: Value from Holman et al. 2011 list via Rama & Wichmann 2020; rationale not verified here. ASJP 3626, glottochronology 4070, GBD 2760 (Rama & Wichmann 2020 Table 5) - the methods disagree strongly.
original_source: Holman et al. 2011, Automated dating of the world's language families based on lexical similarity, Current Anthropology 52(6):841-875 (calibration value as tabulated in Rama & Wichmann 2020 Table 1)
dating_study: Rama & Wichmann 2020, A test of Generalized Bayesian dating, PLOS ONE 15(8):e0236522

node_definition: MRCA of Algonquian excluding Blackfoot (Cree-Innu, Arapahoan, Cheyenne, Menominee, Core Central, Eastern Algonquian); Blackfoot possibly a sister (Goddard 2015)
event: Proto-Algonquian spoken c. 1000-500 BCE, probably immediately west of Lake Superior
controversy_notes: Date is Pentland 1979:329 as reported by Oxford (Routledge handbook chapter); homeland Goddard 1994a. If Blackfoot is included the root must be older. No Bayesian date found.
original_source: Pentland 1979, Algonquian historical phonology (PhD, Univ. of Toronto):329; Goddard 1994a, The west-to-east cline in Algonquian dialectology
dating_study: Oxford, W. (forthcoming/2020s) Algonquian, in Routledge Handbook of North American Languages (preprint, Univ. Manitoba)

node_definition: tip: 17th-c. Massachusett
event: John Eliot's Massachusett Bible (Mamusse Wunneetupanatamwe Up-Biblum God), complete 1663 (NT 1661)
controversy_notes: Large corpus; modern reclamation (Wopanaak) is based on it.
original_source: Eliot, J. 1663. Mamusse Wunneetupanatamwe Up-Biblum God. Cambridge, MA

node_definition: tip: early 17th-c. Powhatan
event: William Strachey's Powhatan vocabulary, compiled c. 1610-1612 (plus John Smith 1612)
controversy_notes: Small (~1000 entries), English-orthography wordlist. Extinct by 18th c.
original_source: Strachey, W. c.1612. The Historie of Travaile into Virginia Britannia (vocabulary)

node_definition: tip: Laurentian 1535-36
event: Vocabularies recorded on Jacques Cartier's second voyage (1535-36), published in the Brief recit (1545)
controversy_notes: ~200 words, partly mixed and transcribed by French speakers; Laurentians disappeared by c. 1580. Its distinctness from Huron and Mohawk also implies Northern Iroquoian diversification well before 1535.
original_source: Cartier, J. 1545. Brief recit et succincte narration de la navigation faicte es ysles de Canada

node_definition: tip: 17th-c. Huron
event: Gabriel Sagard, Le Grand Voyage du pays des Hurons with Dictionaire de la langue huronne (Paris 1632); further Jesuit dictionaries later in the century
controversy_notes: Glottocode wyan1247 = Huron-Wyandot.
original_source: Sagard, G. 1632. Dictionaire de la langue huronne. Paris

node_definition: MRCA of Cherokee (cher1273) and Northern Iroquoian (Mohawk, Seneca, Oneida, Cayuga, Onondaga, Tuscarora, Wyandot...)
event: Split between Southern (Cherokee) and Northern Iroquoian
controversy_notes: Lounsbury 1961 glottochronology 3500-3800 years; a later quantitative study (Julian 2010, PhD diss., Univ. Manitoba) is reported (Wikipedia) to put Proto-Iroquoian c. 2624 BCE (~4570 BP) - not checked in original. No archaeological anchor.
original_source: Lounsbury 1961, Iroquois-Cherokee linguistic relations, in Fenton & Gulick (eds.) Symposium on Cherokee and Iroquois Culture, BAE Bulletin 180
dating_study: Julian 2010, A history of the Iroquoian languages (PhD, Univ. of Manitoba)

node_definition: MRCA of Mississippi Valley Siouan (Dakotan, Chiwere-Winnebago, Dhegiha)
event: ASJP calibration 'Mississippi Valley Siouan' = 2475 years
evidence_type: archaeology/inference (basis in Holman et al. not checked)
controversy_notes: Holman et al. value (years before c. 2000). ASJP 1725, GBD 1760, glottochronology 2404 (Rama & Wichmann 2020 Table 5): both automated methods underestimate.
original_source: Holman et al. 2011, Automated dating of the world's language families based on lexical similarity, Current Anthropology 52(6):841-875 (calibration value as tabulated in Rama & Wichmann 2020 Table 1)
dating_study: Rama & Wichmann 2020, A test of Generalized Bayesian dating, PLOS ONE 15(8):e0236522

node_definition: MRCA of Numic, Takic, Tubatulabal, Hopi (as subgroup recovered by Greenhill et al.)
event: Dispersal of Proto-Northern-Uto-Aztecan unlikely before earliest Mesquite (Prosopis) in the area, ~3490 BP (Fowler 1983; Hill 2015)
evidence_type: inference from reconstructed plant names + palaeobotany
controversy_notes: Greenhill et al. specify lognormal with mean 500 (real space), sigma 0.5, offset 2790; median 3230, 95% 2960-3970 (converted log-mean ln(500)-0.125=6.090). Their BP appears to be relative to c. 2000 CE (see MA-013). Note NUA monophyly itself is debated.
original_source: Fowler 1983, Some lexical clues to Uto-Aztecan prehistory, IJAL 49(3):224-257; Hill 2015
dating_study: Greenhill, Haynie, Ross, Chira, List, Campbell, Botero & Gray 2023, A recent northern origin for the Uto-Aztecan family, Language 99(1):81-107 (calibration section 2.3 of OSF preprint 10.31235/osf.io/k598j)

node_definition: MRCA of Takic (Serrano, Kitanemuk, Gabrielino/Tongva, Cupan: Cahuilla, Cupeno, Luiseno)
event: Population change c. 3000 BP (Sutton 2009); Takic arrival on southern Channel Islands 3000-2500 BP (Kerr 2004); shared fan-palm cognates, palms not in region before 2800 BP (Koehler & Anderson 1995)
controversy_notes: Greenhill et al.: lognormal mean 510 (real space), sigma 0.5, offset 2526; median 2980, 95% 2690-3730. Takic origins 'still under active debate'.
original_source: Sutton 2009; Kerr 2004; Koehler & Anderson 1995 (as cited in Greenhill et al. 2023)
dating_study: Greenhill, Haynie, Ross, Chira, List, Campbell, Botero & Gray 2023, A recent northern origin for the Uto-Aztecan family, Language 99(1):81-107 (calibration section 2.3 of OSF preprint 10.31235/osf.io/k598j)

node_definition: Tubatulabal node (varieties sampled by Greenhill et al.; single-language branch)
event: Continuous Tubatulabal occupation of Kern Plateau / Isabella Basin for 2500 years or longer (Garfinkel 2005)
controversy_notes: Greenhill et al.: lognormal mean 120 (real space), sigma 1, offset 2380; median 2450, 95% 2390-2900. Calibrates the branch (stem) rather than an internal split; continuity-to-language inference is weak.
original_source: Garfinkel 2005 (as cited in Greenhill et al. 2023)
dating_study: Greenhill, Haynie, Ross, Chira, List, Campbell, Botero & Gray 2023, A recent northern origin for the Uto-Aztecan family, Language 99(1):81-107 (calibration section 2.3 of OSF preprint 10.31235/osf.io/k598j)

node_definition: MRCA of Numic (Western: Mono, Northern Paiute; Central: Timbisha, Shoshoni, Comanche; Southern: Kawaiisu, Ute-Southern Paiute)
event: Numic spread linked to traveller-to-processor site transition in southern Sierra Nevada/eastern California, possibly Haiwee Period c. 600 CE (Bettinger & Baumhoff 1982; Garfinkel 2005)
controversy_notes: Greenhill et al.: lognormal mean 120 (real space), sigma 1, offset 1280; median 1350, 95% 1290-1800. The 'Numic spread' archaeological model is itself debated.
original_source: Bettinger & Baumhoff 1982, The Numic spread: Great Basin cultures in competition, American Antiquity 47(3):485-503; Garfinkel 2005
dating_study: Greenhill, Haynie, Ross, Chira, List, Campbell, Botero & Gray 2023, A recent northern origin for the Uto-Aztecan family, Language 99(1):81-107 (calibration section 2.3 of OSF preprint 10.31235/osf.io/k598j)

node_definition: MRCA of all Uto-Aztecan (34 varieties) with Kiowa-Tanoan outgroup
event: Bayesian estimate of Proto-Uto-Aztecan age (Covarion, relaxed clock): mean 4095, 95% HPD 3258-5025 years; strict clocks give ~5300-5400
suggested_distribution: benchmark only (do not use as calibration if NA-016..019, MA-012..013 are used)
controversy_notes: Held-out benchmark. Conflicts: Hill 2001 farming-dispersal 'Ancient Origin' ~8900 BP explicitly rejected; Northern (3000-5000 BP) and Southern (2900-5000 BP) origin hypotheses both compatible. Strict-clock models 1300 years older - clock choice matters more than data here.
original_source: Greenhill et al. 2023
dating_study: Greenhill, Haynie, Ross, Chira, List, Campbell, Botero & Gray 2023, A recent northern origin for the Uto-Aztecan family, Language 99(1):81-107 (calibration section 2.3 of OSF preprint 10.31235/osf.io/k598j)

node_definition: MRCA of Alaskan Inupiaq and Canadian/Greenlandic Inuit
event: Thule eastward migration (13th c. CE) separates Alaskan and eastern Inuit
controversy_notes: Dialect continuum: a tree split is an idealisation (Inuvialuktun/Western Canadian varieties are intermediate). Prefer as a soft bound only.
original_source: Friesen & Arnold 2008
dating_study: Raghavan et al. 2014

node_definition: MRCA of Huastec (huas1242)/Chicomuceltec and all other Mayan
event: First Mayan split (Huastecan departs) c. 2200 BCE per Kaufman; Swadesh's latest possible date 1200 BCE; McQuown 1500 BCE, Manrique 1800 BCE, Dahlin 2100 BCE
controversy_notes: Robertson & Houston argue a later Huastec separation; Kaufman's early date requires *r>y and *q>k to be parallel innovations. Swadesh (via Gruhn) found 32 centuries for Huastec-Yucatec. ASJP dates for Mayan have been criticised as too young.
original_source: Kaufman 1976, Archaeological and linguistic correlations in Mayaland and associated areas of Meso-America, World Archaeology 8(1):101-118

node_definition: MRCA of Ch'olan (Western: Ch'ol, Chontal; Eastern: Ch'olti', Ch'orti')
event: ASJP calibration 'Cholan' = 1600 years
controversy_notes: Holman et al. value (years before c. 2000). Consistent with Houston, Robertson & Stuart 2000 (Classic inscriptions already show Eastern Ch'olan innovations). ASJP 1142, GBD 1246, glottochronology 1599.
original_source: Holman et al. 2011, Automated dating of the world's language families based on lexical similarity, Current Anthropology 52(6):841-875 (calibration value as tabulated in Rama & Wichmann 2020 Table 1)
dating_study: Rama & Wichmann 2020, A test of Generalized Bayesian dating, PLOS ONE 15(8):e0236522

node_definition: tip: language of Classic lowland Maya inscriptions, ancestral to Eastern Ch'olan
event: Hieroglyphic texts of the Classic period (c. 250-900 CE), argued to record a prestige language ancestral to Ch'olti'/Ch'orti'
suggested_distribution: uniform tip age 1050-1700 (or fixed_tip(1350) with sensitivity)
controversy_notes: Lexical coverage of Swadesh-type lists is incomplete and readings evolve; placement as ancestral to Eastern Ch'olan (Houston et al. 2000) is widely but not universally accepted (cf. comment replies, Curr. Anthropol. 2001). Earliest Maya writing at San Bartolo, 300-200 BCE (Saturno et al. 2006, 10.1126/science.1121745), is too sparse for a lexical tip.
original_source: Houston, Robertson & Stuart 2000, The language of Classic Maya inscriptions, Current Anthropology 41(3):321-356

node_definition: tip: colonial Ch'olti' (Manche Ch'ol)
event: Arte y vocabulario de la lengua cholti, MS dated 1695, a copy of Francisco Moran's 'libro grande' (c. 1625-1650); vocabulary ~500 words
controversy_notes: Sole attestation of Ch'olti'.
original_source: Moran, F. MS 1695 (APS Mss.497.4.M79); ed. Robertson, Law & Haertel 2010, Colonial Ch'olti': The Seventeenth-Century Moran Manuscript (Univ. of Oklahoma Press)

node_definition: tip: 16th-17th-c. Yucatec Maya
event: Calepino de Motul (Antonio de Ciudad Real), material from 1577, compiled c. 1580-1614; ~16000 entries
controversy_notes: Choose tip by source; other colonial Yucatec sources (e.g., Beltran 1746 grammar) differ.
original_source: Ciudad Real, A. de. c.1580-1614. Calepino de Motul (ed. Acuna 1984/2001; Arzapalo 1995)

node_definition: tip: 16th-c. Kaqchikel
event: Annals of the Kaqchikels (Memorial de Solola), begun 1571 by Francisco Hernandez Arana Xajila, completed 1604 by Francisco Rojas
controversy_notes: Narrative text, not a wordlist; Swadesh-list extraction needs care.
original_source: Hernandez Arana Xajila & Rojas 1571-1604, Memorial de Solola

node_definition: tip: colonial K'iche'
event: Popol Vuh: original alphabetic K'iche' text usually dated c. 1554-1558 (date not verified here); surviving copy by Francisco Ximenez, Chichicastenango 1701-1703
controversy_notes: Only the Ximenez copy survives; orthography and possible normalisation by the copyist.
original_source: Ximenez, F. c.1701-1703, Popol Vuh MS (Newberry Library, Ayer MS 1515)

node_definition: MRCA of Mixean and Zoquean (incl. Sayula/Oluta Popoluca, Tapachultec)
event: Proto-Mixe-Zoque associated with the Olmec (San Lorenzo, c. 1500-1200 BCE)
controversy_notes: Olmec=Mixe-Zoque association (Campbell & Kaufman 1976) is widely cited but contested; the specific date (often given as c. 1500 BCE) not verified in the original here. ASJP dates for Mixe-Zoquean were criticised as too young (Rama & Wichmann 2020 discussion).
original_source: Campbell & Kaufman 1976, A linguistic look at the Olmecs, American Antiquity 41(1):80-89

node_definition: tip: language of La Mojarra Stela 1 / Tuxtla Statuette, claimed pre-Proto-Zoquean
event: Long Count dates on La Mojarra Stela 1: 143 CE and 156 CE; Tuxtla Statuette Long Count 8.6.2.4.17 (162 CE)
controversy_notes: Justeson & Kaufman 1993/1997 decipherment as pre-Proto-Zoquean; disputed by Houston & Coe (Mexicon 25, 2003/04). If accepted, implies Mixean-Zoquean split before c. 150 CE. Statuette date not re-verified here.
original_source: Justeson & Kaufman 1993, A decipherment of Epi-Olmec hieroglyphic writing, Science 259:1703-1711
dating_study: Kaufman & Justeson 1997, Science 277:207-210

node_definition: MRCA of all Otomanguean (Otopamean, Chinantecan, Tlapanecan, Mixtecan, Popolocan, Zapotecan, Amuzgo, Chorotegan)
event: Proto-Otomanguean spoken before 2000 BCE (Kaufman & Justeson 2009); glottochronology c. 4400 BCE (Campbell 1997:159); Tehuacan culture possibly Otomanguean
controversy_notes: Deepest-dated family in the Americas on glottochronology alone. Kaufman & Justeson give only a terminus ante quem. No Bayesian dating found.
original_source: Kaufman & Justeson 2009, Historical linguistics and pre-Columbian Mesoamerica, Ancient Mesoamerica 20(2):221-231
dating_study: Campbell 1997, American Indian Languages (OUP), p.159

node_definition: tip: 16th-c. Zapotec
event: Juan de Cordova, Vocabulario en lengua capoteca and Arte en lengua zapoteca (Mexico 1578)
controversy_notes: Zapotec script inscriptions (Monte Alban) are undeciphered and unusable as lexical tips.
original_source: Cordova, J. de. 1578. Vocabulario en lengua capoteca. Mexico

node_definition: MRCA of Nahuan (Pochutec, Classical Nahuatl and modern Nahuatl varieties)
event: Nahuan entry into central Mexico relative to the fall of Teotihuacan (~500 CE); Kaufman 2001 suggests origins c. 400 BCE to account for Mixe-Zoque/Huastec/Totonac contact
controversy_notes: Greenhill et al.: lognormal mean 290 (real space), sigma 0.7, offset 1510; median 1740, 95% 1570-2410. Pre- vs post-Teotihuacan Nahua presence is actively debated (Kaufman 2001; Dakin & Wichmann 2000; Pharao Hansen 2024 Nahuatl Nations, OUP).
original_source: Kaufman 2001, The history of the Nawa language group from the earliest times to the sixteenth century (ms.); Suarez 1983
dating_study: Greenhill, Haynie, Ross, Chira, List, Campbell, Botero & Gray 2023, A recent northern origin for the Uto-Aztecan family, Language 99(1):81-107 (calibration section 2.3 of OSF preprint 10.31235/osf.io/k598j)

node_definition: tip: 16th-c. Classical Nahuatl
event: Alonso de Molina, Vocabulario (1555; expanded Vocabulario en lengua castellana y mexicana 1571)
controversy_notes: Greenhill et al. used a tip of 445 years BP = years before 2000 CE for 1555; on a 1950 basis this is 395 BP. Check the BP basis of all Greenhill et al. calibrations before reuse (+/-50 y).
original_source: Molina, A. de. 1555/1571. Vocabulario en lengua castellana y mexicana. Mexico
dating_study: Greenhill, Haynie, Ross, Chira, List, Campbell, Botero & Gray 2023, A recent northern origin for the Uto-Aztecan family, Language 99(1):81-107 (calibration section 2.3 of OSF preprint 10.31235/osf.io/k598j)

node_definition: tip: earliest Nahuatl grammar
event: Andres de Olmos, Arte de la lengua mexicana (1547)
controversy_notes: Grammar rather than lexicon; same tip as MA-013 for most purposes.
original_source: Olmos, A. de. 1547. Arte de la lengua mexicana (MS)

node_definition: tip: 16th-c. Mixtec (Teposcolula)
event: Francisco de Alvarado, Vocabulario en lengua misteca (Mexico 1593); Antonio de los Reyes, Arte en lengua mixteca (1593)
controversy_notes: Mixtec is a dialect complex; colonial Teposcolula variety must be matched to modern varieties.
original_source: Alvarado, F. de. 1593. Vocabulario en lengua misteca. Mexico

node_definition: tip: 16th-c. Tarascan
event: Maturino Gilberti, Arte de la lengua de Michuacan (1558) and Vocabulario en lengua de Mechuacan (1559)
controversy_notes: Isolate (Tarascan): useful only for within-Purepecha dialect dating or rate calibration of a single lineage.
original_source: Gilberti, M. 1559. Vocabulario en lengua de Mechuacan. Mexico

node_definition: split of Taino from its closest Caribbean-Arawakan sister(s) (pre-Taino node calibration)
event: First permanent Saladoid settlements in Greater/N. Lesser Antilles (Montserrat, Nevis, Puerto Rico, Vieques) 2450-2445 BP; earliest Saladoid finds in Greater Antilles 2800-2220 BP

dating_study: Campbell L (2012) Classification of the indigenous languages of South America. In Grondona & Campbell (eds) The Indigenous Languages of South America, De Gruyter, 59-166 (reporting Constenla Umana 2005, Estudios de Linguistica Chibcha 23:9-59)

node_definition: tip: Mapudungun
event: Valdivia L de (1606) Arte y gramatica general de la lengua que corre en todo el Reyno de Chile (Lima)
controversy_notes: Family has only Mapudungun + Huilliche; tip useful for pooled rates. Febres (1765) is a second colonial source.
original_source: Valdivia L de (1606) Arte y gramatica... Lima

node_definition: tip: Cholon
event: Mata P de la (1748) Arte de la lengua cholona (ms, British Library; copy by Clota 1772)
original_source: Mata P de la (1748) Arte de la lengua cholona; ed. Alexander-Bakkerus

node_definition: tip: Kipea (Kariri)
event: Mamiani L V (1698) Catecismo; (1699) Arte de grammatica da lingua brasilica da naçam Kiriri (Lisbon)
controversy_notes: Kariri membership in Macro-Je is a hypothesis (Ribeiro, Nikulin). Publication dates not re-verified online this session (Glottolog gives first documentation 1698).
original_source: Mamiani LV (1699) Arte de grammatica da lingua brasilica da naçam Kiriri. Lisbon

node_definition: tip: Lule
event: Machoni de Cerdena A (1732) Arte y vocabulario de la lengua lule y tonocote (Madrid)
controversy_notes: Lule-Vilela relation itself debated.
original_source: Machoni A (1732) Arte y vocabulario de la lengua lule y tonocote. Madrid

node_definition: tip: Abipon (extinct)
event: Dobrizhoffer M (1784) Historia de Abiponibus (Vienna)
controversy_notes: Gives an extinct Southern Guaicuruan tip next to Toba, Mocovi, Pilaga.
original_source: Dobrizhoffer M (1784) Historia de Abiponibus. Vienna

node_definition: tip: Galibi Carib
event: Pelleprat P (1655) Introduction a la langue des Galibis (Paris)
controversy_notes: Short grammar sketch (c. 30 pp.); 1763 Paris dictionary also drew on it.
original_source: Pelleprat P (1655) Introduction a la langue des Galibis. Paris: Cramoisy

node_definition: tip: Cumana-branch Cariban
event: Ruiz Blanco M (1690) Conversion de Piritu (Cumanagoto); Yangues (1683) and Tauste (1680, Chaima) grammars
controversy_notes: 1690 Ruiz Blanco is confirmed; 1680 (Tauste) and 1683 (Yangues) dates were not confirmed this session (only Platzmann 1888 facsimiles found).
original_source: Ruiz Blanco M (1690) Conversion de Piritu. Madrid

node_definition: Tukanoan root (Eastern vs Western Tukanoan)
event: Relative internal diversity 2500-3000 years; glottochronology 2400 years (Swadesh 100, r=14/1000); ASJP 2699 years; Proto-WT and Proto-ET each c. 1000 BP
controversy_notes: From conference slides only, not peer-reviewed; Chacon & List (2015) Bayesian tree is published but no node ages were found. Published estimate, benchmark only - circular if used as calibration.
original_source: Chacon T, 'The Vaupes from a Tukanoan prism' (slides, MPI-SHH; undated)

node_definition: Southern Je lineage vs Taquara-Itararé tradition (proto-Southern-Je archaeology)
event: Taquara-Itararé ceramics and pit-house villages in southern Brazilian highlands (Araucaria expansion); coastal Itararé-Taquara in shell mounds c. 1300-500 BP
controversy_notes: Association with Southern Je speakers is widely accepted (de Souza, Iriarte, Noelli) but no specific onset date was verified this session. No published dated phylogeny for Je/Macro-Je found (Nikulin 2020 is a reconstruction without dates).
original_source: Iriarte J, Behling H (2007) Environmental Archaeology; de Souza JG et al. (2016) PLOS ONE (Baggio I) [dates not checked]

node_definition: MRCA of Wati (Western Desert) languages, e.g. Pitjantjatjara, Ngaanyatjarra, Martu Wangka, Pintupi-Luritja, Kukatja
event: Expansion of Wati speakers into current Western Desert range; occupation from as early as ~5 ka to 1.5 ka, peak activity 3-2.5 ka
suggested_distribution: offset_lognormal_node(3000,6.37,0.64) + hard_minimum(1500)  [original: offset-gamma offset 3000, alpha=2, beta(scale)=359, 95% HPD 3000-5000, plus breakup no later than 1.5 ka]
controversy_notes: The ONLY node calibration in Bouckaert et al. 2018; the root age scales roughly linearly with it. Paper uses 'ka' before present, not stated as 1950-based (difference negligible). Archaeology dates occupation of the Western Desert, not the Wati split itself; linking is inferential. Other candidate calibrations (Queensland, Victoria, Lake Eyre Basin, offshore islands) were rejected as not linkable to nodes.
original_source: Veth/Smith Western Desert archaeology as cited (refs 13,74,75) in Bouckaert et al. 2018
dating_study: Bouckaert, Bowern & Atkinson 2018, The origin and expansion of Pama-Nyungan languages across Australia, Nat Ecol Evol 2:741-749

node_definition: MRCA of all Pama-Nyungan languages (306 languages sampled)
event: Posterior root age of Pama-Nyungan, homeland south of the Gulf of Carpentaria
controversy_notes: Posterior estimate, not an independent calibration: depends entirely on AU-01 plus tip sampling times; use only as held-out benchmark (do not combine with AU-01). Supports mid-Holocene rapid-replacement hypothesis over Pleistocene-origin hypotheses.
dating_study: Bouckaert, Bowern & Atkinson 2018, Nat Ecol Evol 2:741-749

node_definition: Split between any Tasmanian language lineage and any mainland Australian lineage (only meaningful if a relationship is assumed)
event: Final flooding of the Bassian land bridge isolating Tasmania; last possible walking crossing at least 11,960 and likely ~12,425 years ago (Hamacher et al. 2023); older estimates ~14,000 BP for first major breach
controversy_notes: Bowern 2012 finds Tasmanian wordlists form ~5 clusters NOT demonstrably related to each other or to mainland languages, so this bound rarely attaches to a tree node. Ages are years before present (not explicitly 1950-based). Some sources give ~8,000 BP (outlier). Bound is 'split no later than' isolation.
original_source: Hamacher, Nunn, Gantevoort, Taylor, Lehman, Law & Miles 2023, The archaeology of orality: dating Tasmanian Aboriginal oral traditions to the Late Pleistocene, J Archaeol Sci
dating_study: Bowern 2012, The riddle of Tasmanian languages, Proc R Soc B 279:4590-4595 (relationship caveat)

node_definition: Sydney language as recorded by William Dawes (Port Jackson), informant Patyegarang
event: Dawes notebooks, 1790-1791 (SOAS MS 41645)
controversy_notes: Earliest substantial Sydney-area record; corpus is fragmentary (lexicon and phrases), so many Swadesh slots may be missing. Language name not recorded by Dawes; 'Dharug/Dharuk' is conventional.
original_source: Dawes, W. 1790-1791. Notebooks on the Aboriginal language of Sydney. SOAS MS 41645 (facsimile 2009, Hans Rausing ELP)

node_definition: Guugu Yimidhirr (Endeavour River, Cooktown)
event: Cook and Banks record words incl. 'kangooroo' at Endeavour River, July-August 1770 (Banks journal 4 Aug 1770)
suggested_distribution: fixed_tip(180) only for those few items; use modern documentation (Haviland 1970s) otherwise
controversy_notes: Only a handful of words; unusable as a full-wordlist tip date. Useful as attestation check for individual cognate sets.
original_source: Banks, J. 1770 Endeavour journal; Cook, J. 1770 journal

node_definition: Tasmanian languages (Bowern 2012: ~12 languages in 5 clusters)
event: Wordlists recorded by explorers, missionaries, convicts etc. between 1777 and 1847 (compiled by Plomley 1976)
controversy_notes: Per-wordlist dates vary; orthographies inconsistent; language identity of lists uncertain.
original_source: Plomley, N.J.B. 1976, A word-list of the Tasmanian Aboriginal languages
dating_study: Bowern 2012, Proc R Soc B 279:4590-4595

node_definition: Kaurna (Adelaide Plains)
event: Teichelmann & Schurmann grammar and vocabulary, Adelaide, 1840
controversy_notes: Publication date from general knowledge, not re-verified in this session; Kaurna is now under revival, so modern lists are not independent tips.
original_source: Teichelmann, C.G. & Schurmann, C.W. 1840, Outlines of a grammar, vocabulary, and phraseology of the aboriginal language of South Australia

node_definition: MRCA of Trans New Guinea languages (300-500 languages; core highland subgroups)
event: Initial dispersal of TNG languages associated with the spread of agriculture through the major highland valleys, 'perhaps between 10,000 and 6,000 years ago'
suggested_distribution: uniform_node(6000,10000) (soft edges) ; benchmark rather than calibration
controversy_notes: No Bayesian dated phylogeny of TNG exists to my knowledge; time depth is a hedged scenario. Family membership itself is debated. Do not use as a hard bound.
original_source: Pawley 2005, The chequered career of the Trans New Guinea hypothesis, in Pawley et al. (eds) Papuan Pasts, Pacific Linguistics 572: 67-107
dating_study: Pawley & Hammarstrom 2018, The Trans New Guinea family, in Palmer (ed.) The Languages and Linguistics of the New Guinea Area, De Gruyter Mouton: 21-195

target: TNG max bound via Kuk agriculture
node_definition: MRCA of TNG (under agricultural-dispersal hypothesis only)
event: Kuk Swamp: plant exploitation/cultivation 10,220-9910 cal BP (phase 1); mounded cultivation by 6950-6440 cal BP (phase 2); ditched cultivation by 4350-3980 cal BP (phase 3)
suggested_distribution: soft_maximum(10220,1000) only if TNG-agriculture link assumed
controversy_notes: Denham reads agriculture from 6950-6440 cal BP; Golson & Hughes from ~10,000 cal BP. Linking TNG dispersal to Kuk is a hypothesis, not evidence; bound direction (TNG no older than agriculture) holds only if dispersal was agricultural.
original_source: Denham et al. 2003, Origins of agriculture at Kuk Swamp in the Highlands of New Guinea, Science 301:189-193
dating_study: Pawley & Hammarstrom 2018 (linkage)

node_definition: MRCA of Tok Pisin, Bislama, Solomons Pijin
event: Common Pacific pidgin pool from Queensland labour trade (from 1863) differentiates; Samoan plantation variety (1879-1912) feeds Tok Pisin; NH/Solomons recruits to Samoa stop after ~1885
controversy_notes: CREOLE CAVEAT: not tree-like (lexifier English + Oceanic substrate, ongoing contact). Keesing 1988 argues stabilization already in the 1840s (~110 BP) from whaling/trade jargon and that Queensland and Samoan varieties were near-identical, against Muhlhausler's separate-development view. Tok Pisin glottocode from general knowledge.
original_source: Tryon & Charpentier 2004, Pacific Pidgins and Creoles: Origins, Growth and Development, De Gruyter
dating_study: Keesing 1988, Melanesian Pidgin and the Oceanic Substrate, Stanford UP (conflicting view)

node_definition: MRCA of Pitkern (Pitcairn) and Norfuk (Norfolk Island)
event: Bounty mutineers and Tahitians settle Pitcairn 1790; ~193-194 Pitcairners moved to Norfolk Island 1856; 16 returned 1858, four families 1864
controversy_notes: CREOLE CAVEAT: English + Tahitian contact language; creole status contested. Back-migration 1858/1864 means post-split gene flow. Norfuk later influenced by Australian English. Very small populations: strong drift.
original_source: Ross & Moverley 1964, The Pitcairnese Language; Mühlhäusler 2020 Pitkern-Norf'k (De Gruyter)

node_definition: MRCA of Sranan and Saramaccan (Saramaccan and Matawai from early Sranan/Dju-Tongo)
event: English colony 1651-1667 (max); Dutch takeover 1667; Portuguese-relexified 'Dju-Tongo' on Jewish plantations 1675-1680; first mass escapes forming the Saramaccan 1690-1695; Saramaccan structure fixed early 18th c.
controversy_notes: CREOLE CAVEAT: Saramaccan has heavy Portuguese and Gbe/Kikongo components, not a clean tree split. Britannica places Saramaccan crystallization in early 18th c., ApICS gives escapes 1690-1695.
original_source: Smith 1987, The genesis of the creole languages of Surinam (PhD, Amsterdam); Price 1983, First-Time
dating_study: Arends 2017, Language and Slavery: a social and linguistic history of the Suriname creoles, Benjamins (CLL 52); ApICS survey 3 (Saramaccan)

node_definition: MRCA of Sranan and Ndyuka (Eastern Maroon Creole)
event: Ndyuka maroon formation in early 18th c.; peace treaty with colony 1760
controversy_notes: Dates from general knowledge of Suriname maroon history; not verified in this session. CREOLE CAVEAT applies.
original_source: Price 1983; Arends 2017 (to verify)

node_definition: MRCA of Mauritian Creole and Seychelles Creole
event: Mauritius French settlement 1721 (max); Seychelles settled 27 Aug 1770 mainly from Mauritius, also Reunion; settlers brought stabilized Mauritian Creole
controversy_notes: CREOLE CAVEAT. ApICS: Seychellois an offshoot of Mauritian, still mutually intelligible; later Reunion slave imports (1778+) and continued Mauritius contact mean the 1770 date is a split start, not isolation.
original_source: ApICS survey 56 (Seychelles Creole), citing Baker 1982
dating_study: Michaelis et al. (eds) 2013, Atlas of Pidgin and Creole Language Structures Online (apics-online.info)

node_definition: Papiamentu (Curacao)
event: Earliest known Papiamentu text: private love letter of 1775 (~150 words, by a Curacaoan Sephardic Jew); 1776 dialogue; 1783 Schermer-Charje letters
controversy_notes: CREOLE CAVEAT. Text very short; not a full wordlist. Glottocode from general knowledge.
original_source: Leiden 'Letters as Loot' corpus; Van der Wal 2011 (1783 letters)

node_definition: Berbice Dutch Creole (Guyana; Eastern Ijo substrate)
event: Documented by Robertson and Kouwenberg (fieldwork 1970s-1990s; Kouwenberg 1994 grammar); last speaker Albertha Bell interviewed 2004, d. 2005; declared extinct Feb 2010
controversy_notes: CREOLE CAVEAT; strongly mixed lexicon (Dutch + Eastern Ijo). Berbice colony from 1627 is max bound on the creole. Kouwenberg 1994 date from general knowledge.
original_source: Kouwenberg 1994, A Grammar of Berbice Dutch Creole, Mouton de Gruyter; ApICS survey 28

node_definition: Negerhollands (Virgin Islands Dutch Creole)
event: Danish West Indies (St Thomas from 1672); 18th-c. Moravian texts; last speaker died late 1980s
controversy_notes: Exact text dates and 1987 death date not verified this session (a 1992 paper says the last speaker 'died recently'). CREOLE CAVEAT.
original_source: to verify (e.g. van Rossem & van der Voort 1996, Die Creol Taal)

node_definition: MRCA of Ternate (Cavite) Chabacano and Zamboanga Chabacano
event: Ternateno Merdicas withdrawn from Ternate (Moluccas) ~1660 and settled on Manila Bay (Ternate, Cavite) 1663 (other sources 1674); Zamboanga variety said to form from ~1635 (weak source)
controversy_notes: Whinnom-style monogenesis (Zamboangueño from Manila Bay creole) vs independent formation is debated; 1635 Zamboanga date from a weak web source. Ternate considered earliest Chabacano variety (ApICS 44). CREOLE CAVEAT.
original_source: ApICS survey 44 (Ternate Chabacano)

node_definition: Palenquero (San Basilio de Palenque, Colombia) divergence from Cartagena-area contact varieties
event: Maroon settlement founded c. 1599-1603 (Benkos Bioho); 1605 truce; royal recognition decree 1713
controversy_notes: Dates come mostly from popular sources; Palenquero is Spanish-lexified with Kikongo component, Portuguese-influence claims debated. Not a tree node in a standard sense. CREOLE CAVEAT.
original_source: to verify against Schwegler (e.g. 1996) / ApICS Palenquero survey

node_definition: Hawaii Creole English (Pidgin) as distinct from Hawaii Pidgin English
event: Creole emerges among locally born children of plantation immigrants c. 1905-1920
controversy_notes: Roberts 1998 argues creole arose locally ~1905-1920 via diffusion; disputed by Bickerton-style accounts (date of creolization contested, cf. reply letter in Language 1998). CREOLE CAVEAT.
original_source: Roberts 1998, The role of diffusion in the genesis of Hawaiian Creole, Language 74(1):1-39

node_definition: MRCA of Afrikaans and (Holland) Dutch
event: Dutch East India Company station at the Cape founded by Van Riebeeck, 1652
controversy_notes: Max bound is firm; but Afrikaans is a partially restructured (semi-creole) language with Malay, Portuguese creole, Khoekhoe influence; continued contact with Dutch until 19th-20th c. as standard language. Split age ~ founding date if Cape Dutch treated as a colony offshoot.
original_source: Standard historical record (VOC Cape settlement 1652)

node_definition: MRCA of Brazilian and European Portuguese varieties
event: Portuguese landfall 1500; first permanent settlement Sao Vicente 1532; continuous migration through 19th-20th c.
controversy_notes: Dialect divergence under continuous migration and standard-language contact; not a clean split. Use only as max bound. Glottolog does not separate the two as languages.
original_source: Standard historical record

node_definition: MRCA of Quebec French and metropolitan French
event: Quebec City founded 1608; French immigration mostly 1608-1760; British conquest 1760/Treaty of Paris 1763 ends French settler inflow
controversy_notes: Settler founders mainly from NW France (koine formation in 17th c.); ongoing standard-French influence. Acadian (Port-Royal 1605) is a separate branch.
original_source: Standard historical record

node_definition: MRCA of American and British English varieties
event: Jamestown 1607, Plymouth 1620; independence 1776
controversy_notes: Continuous contact, migration and print standardization; colonial lag hypotheses; usable only as weak max bound or benchmark of near-zero lexical divergence.
original_source: Standard historical record

node_definition: Cape Verdean Creole (all varieties: Sotavento incl. Santiago; Barlavento incl. Sao Vicente)
event: Settlement of Santiago (Ribeira Grande) from 1462 (max for creole); later settlement of Barlavento islands (Sao Vicente mostly late 18th-19th c.) for Sotavento/Barlavento split
controversy_notes: Santiago 1462 from general knowledge, not re-verified this session; Barlavento-Sotavento split dates not verified (grade for that sub-claim U). CREOLE CAVEAT; relationship to Guinea-Bissau Kriyol (Upper Guinea Creole) also relevant.
original_source: to verify (e.g. Baptista; ApICS Cape Verdean surveys)

node_definition: MRCA of Rioplatense Spanish and Peninsular Spanish
event: Buenos Aires founded 1536 (abandoned 1541), refounded 1580
controversy_notes: Dialect-level; massive Italian immigration 1880-1930; continuous contact. Benchmark only. Dates from general knowledge.
original_source: Standard historical record
